title: The Best Way to Learn a Codebase Is to Break Someone Else's
description: What maintainers of kitty, calibre, libtorrent and Fallow taught me in review threads, usually by explaining why my fix was wrong in a way I hadn't considered.
text: I started sending pull requests to open-source projects in March 2026, mostly to tools I use every day. At the time of writing that's  merged, across Python, C++, Rust, Go and shell. (The full list is generated from GitHub, so it can't flatter me.)I learned more from the review threads than from the code I wrote, mostly from maintainers telling me, politely, that I'd missed something about their project that nobody could have told me in advance.The bug that was a decisionIn kitty's drag-and-drop kitten, local copies used hard links when they could. That looked like a bug to me: edit the destination and you've edited the source too. I wrote it up as a fix.Kovid Goyal's answer was that he'd chosen hard links deliberately, for performance, and that for a move they were always right. For a copy it was debatable, so perhaps an option. The PR became an opt-in independent copy mode with the default left alone, and it merged.Since then, before I "fix" something odd in a mature codebase, I check whether it's odd on purpose. The git blame or the maintainer usually knows.The fix that was too expensiveIn calibre I wrote a shared guard to keep user-supplied paths inside the library root. My first version resolved every path with realpath().The review pointed out that realpath() does filesystem I/O, and that many of the paths I'd touched didn't need it. Inside calibre's own library directory you can assume there are no symlinks, because calibre doesn't create them. A security fix that slows down every path check has a cost, and knowing which invariants a codebase already guarantees lets you avoid most of it.The optimization that could go furtherIn libtorrent I sped up the piece picker's bitfield updates for sparse bitfields. Arvid Norberg benchmarked it and called it a significant improvement to piece-picker performance, then suggested going further: make the visitor a member of the bitfield type so it can skip zeroes a word at a time instead of a byte at a time. He also caught that I'd used std::countl_zero without including <bit>, which only showed up when the installed headers were compiled on their own. I wouldn't have known to look for either.Maintainers are people with too little timeSome of the threads that changed how I contribute weren't about code at all.In Docling I opened a PR for an issue someone else had already fixed the night before. The maintainer thanked me anyway and asked that next time I comment on the issue before starting, so they could assign it, which is obvious in hindsight. I do open source in the gaps around a day job, and claiming the issue first is how you stop two people spending those gaps on the same thing.In Fallow, one of my PRs sat for a while with a failing check I had no way to fix myself. When it merged, Bart Waardenburg apologized for the wait and explained what that check was, so it wouldn't look like my problem next time. On another PR he pushed his own review fixes to my branch and noted that my newest commits had replaced his local versions of the same fixes. I've learned a fair amount about running a project from being on the receiving end of that.What carried over between projectsReading before writing carries over. For my first large Fallow PR, which taught it to understand Vue and Nuxt conventions (about 1,100 lines across 44 files), I read the whole analysis pipeline before changing anything: the graph builder, the import resolver, the framework detection. Most of the time went into working out what the codebase assumed; the change itself came after.Idioms don't. My early Rust had Python in it: deep nesting, mutable state, strings where the codebase used enums. Nobody rewrote it for me; reviewers showed the idiomatic version and why it was preferred, and that's why it stuck.If you want to startPick a tool you use every day and wait for it to annoy you. Read the issue tracker to see whether someone's already on it, say you're taking it, and read the surrounding code before you touch anything. The fix might take an hour, and understanding the code well enough to make it might take a day. I've learned most from the day.And when a maintainer says no, read the reason twice. It's usually the most useful thing in the thread.

title: Every Abstraction I Regret
description: A short list of abstractions I added too early, why they got worse over time, and the heuristics I use now to avoid repeating it.
text:
The best code I ever deleted was a utility function called format_response. It accepted a response object, a format string, a fallback value, an optional transformer function, and a boolean for whether to strip whitespace. It was used in one place.I wrote it because I thought I'd need it again, and I never did. It sat in utils.py for eight months, collecting type: ignore comments and confusing every developer who opened the file.This post is about the abstractions I built too early and the DRY violations that would have been better left wet.The Generic Service Layer That Served NobodyEarly in Polaris, I built a "generic" service layer. The idea was that every model gets a service class with standard CRUD operations, validation hooks, and permission checks, written once and inherited everywhere.class BaseService:
    model = None
    serializer = None

    def create(self, data, **kwargs):
        self._validate(data)
        self._check_permissions(kwargs.get('user'))
        instance = self.model.objects.create(**data)
        self._post_create(instance)
        return instance

    def _validate(self, data):
        pass  # Override in subclass

    def _check_permissions(self, user):
        pass  # Override in subclass

    def _post_create(self, instance):
        pass  # Override in subclassEvery subclass overrode every method. ProductService._validate had nothing in common with CustomerService._validate. The "shared" base class was an empty method contract that added indirection without reducing duplication.When I needed behavior that didn't fit the create/read/update/delete pattern, like Polaris's FIFO inventory consumption or double-entry ledger operations, the service layer fought me. It assumed every operation was CRUD, and financial operations aren't.What Replaced ItI replaced it with individual service classes and no shared base. LedgerService has credit_customer and reverse. InventoryService has consume_inventory and receive_batch. They share nothing because they do nothing in common.By DRY standards the code is "less clean", and it's much easier to understand and modify.Django Signals for EverythingThe performance log covers what signals did to Polaris's speed. Debugging them was worse.At one point, creating a sale in Polaris triggered a chain like this:post_save on Sale → update inventorypost_save on Product (from #1) → recalculate stock alertspost_save on StockAlert (from #2) → notify supplierpost_save on Sale (again) → update customer balanceCustom signal balance_changed → invalidate cached reportsGood luck tracing a bug through that. There's no call stack and no explicit invocation. grep finds the handler but not what triggers it, because signals are implicit coupling disguised as decoupling.What Replaced ItI replaced them with explicit function calls.class SaleService:
    def complete_sale(self, sale):
        with transaction.atomic():
            self._deduct_inventory(sale)
            self._update_customer_balance(sale)
            self._invalidate_reports(sale.customer_id)By separation-of-concerns standards this is "worse", since SaleService now knows about inventory and reporting. But anyone reading complete_sale can trace the whole execution path without leaving the function, and I'll take that over architectural purity.When Signals Make SenseSignals belong at app boundaries where loose coupling matters. Your billing app doesn't need to know about your analytics app, so a "payment completed" signal is fine when the handler lives in a different bounded context.Inside a single app's core business logic, they mostly serve the architecture diagram.The "Reusable" Component LibraryIn a frontend project, I built a component library before I had components to put in it: a BaseCard with 12 props, and a BaseButton with configurable size, variant, icon position, loading state, and disabled tooltip.BaseCard was used in 3 places across the project, each with a completely different layout that made the "base" props irrelevant. Two of the three instances passed so many overrides that the component was essentially a <div> with extra steps.The button was worse. I added a tooltipPosition prop because one button needed a left-aligned tooltip. Now every button in the system carries tooltip positioning logic it doesn't use. The component API grew to accommodate every edge case, which meant every consumer had to understand the whole API when all they wanted was a button.What I Do NowI start with the raw HTML elements, and I only extract the shared part once I have three similar components with non-trivial logic in common.<!-- Three similar buttons? Copy-paste is fine until it isn't. -->
<button class="btn-primary" @click="save">Save</button>
<button class="btn-primary" @click="submit">Submit</button>
<button class="btn-primary" :disabled="loading" @click="confirm">
  {{ loading ? 'Confirming...' : 'Confirm' }}
</button>The third button has a loading state. That's one button, and no reason for a component library.The Config-Driven ArchitectureAt one point, I tried to make Polaris "configurable" by externalizing business rules into configuration objects:INVENTORY_CONFIG = {
    "costing_method": "fifo",
    "allow_negative_stock": False,
    "reorder_threshold_multiplier": 1.5,
    "batch_tracking_enabled": True,
    "auto_reorder_enabled": False,
}The idea was that different clients could customize behavior without code changes. Just update the config!Every "configuration" eventually needed code changes anyway. "Allow negative stock" sounds like a boolean, but the business logic for negative stock is very different from positive-stock-only logic. It needs its own code path, with its own validation, reporting, and financial implications.I ended up with code riddled with if settings.INVENTORY_CONFIG["allow_negative_stock"]: branches, each one tested independently and each one a possible bug. The config took the complexity and spread it across every function that read it.What Replaced ItI went back to hard-coded business rules that match the client's requirements. When a new client needs different behavior, I work out whether it's a real variation or a different product. Usually it's a different product.Configuration is for deployment parameters: database URLs, API keys, feature flags for A/B tests. Business rules are code. They deserve tests, type checking, and code review, none of which work well on a dict of settings.The Pattern I Keep Coming Back ToEvery abstraction I regret was built for a need I only expected to have. The generic service layer was for "when we have 50 models." The config-driven architecture was for "when we have multiple clients." The component library was for "when we have a design system."None of those futures arrived the way I imagined, and when they arrived at all, the requirements were different enough that the abstraction didn't fit.The abstractions I don't regret were all extracted from code that already existed. I wrote the code three times, noticed the pattern, and pulled it out. TenantAwareQuerySet in Polaris started as copy-pasted .filter(organization=org) calls. When I had 15 models all doing the same filter, the abstraction was obvious and correct.My rule now is that if you can't point to three existing call sites that would use the abstraction, you're speculating. Speculation in code is expensive because it's permanent until someone is brave enough to delete it.And deleting abstractions is harder than deleting regular code. Regular code has no dependents. An abstraction has consumers, each of which was shaped by the abstraction's API. Removing it means refactoring every consumer, so it tends to stay.So when you're about to create BaseService, GenericHandler, or AbstractProcessor, write the specific thing first, and write it again when you need it again. By the third time you'll have seen what the abstraction is.

title: Scoring Fraud in Legal Intake Calls
description: Coached callers, invented doctors and borrowed photos. How RISQ scores intake calls for mass tort firms, and why the most useful score is the one that grades the interviewer.
text: Mass tort firms run intake lines that take a lot of calls from people who may qualify for a case: they took a certain drug, had a certain device implanted, lived near a certain plant. Some share of those callers aren't who they say they are. Some are coached and reading from a script, some never used the product, and some call back under a different name.RISQ listens to those calls, scores them, and recommends one of three things: send the caller on to a closer, flag them for a human to review, or quarantine the call. This post covers how the scoring works in principle. The weights and thresholds belong to the client, so they're not here.Four questions, asked separatelyRISQ asks four separate questions and combines the answers at the end:Recall: does the caller remember the texture of what happened to them? When, where, who treated them, what it felt like.Integrity: does the call sound like a real person telling their own story, or does it carry the markers of a script?Qualification: does the caller meet this campaign's legal criteria?Session: did the intake agent ask good questions?The first three feed the recommendation. The fourth doesn't, and it ended up mattering more than the other three.Scoring the interviewerA bad intake interview makes honest callers look suspicious. If the agent asks leading questions ("you took this between 2018 and 2020, right?"), a real claimant's answers sound rehearsed, because the agent rehearsed them. If the agent skips the questions that would reveal real recall, the caller never gets the chance to show it.So the session score sits as a gate in front of everything else. If the interview was poor, RISQ makes no recommendation about the caller and marks the call for re-screening. That gate prevented more wrongly quarantined callers than any other change we made.Decisions as a series of gatesThe recommendation comes from a sequence of gates, and a call leaves at the first one it fails:Hard disqualifiers from the campaign rules.The session gate above.Minimums on integrity and qualification that no composite can make up for.A check for the coaching pattern described below.Only then, the combined score mapped to transfer, review or quarantine.Ordering it this way keeps the explanations honest. When a call is quarantined, the reviewer sees which gate it failed alongside the number.The perfect caller problemCoached callers have a signature. They know what qualifies them, because someone told them, so their qualification looks excellent. They can't fill in the details around it, though: the pharmacy, what the pills looked like, what else was going on that year. High qualification with thin recall is suspicious in a way that neither score is on its own, so RISQ checks for that combination explicitly.What happens to one callThe call is transcribed with speaker separation. The caller's words have to be kept apart from the agent's, or the agent's phrasing leaks into the caller's scores.An LLM then reads the transcript and pulls out structured claims: which product, when, which symptoms, which doctors and facilities. Each claim carries a confidence level. The same pass flags language signals, like dates that are oddly exact while everything around them is vague, legal vocabulary most people wouldn't use, and contradictions between the start and end of the call.Named doctors are checked against the NPI registry for existence and specialty, and named facilities against CMS provider data. "Dr. Smith at Memorial Hospital" either exists with the right specialty or doesn't.For some campaigns the caller is asked by text to send a photo of the packaging, a prescription label or a record. A vision model checks that the image is what it claims to be and isn't a stock photo or someone else's paperwork.Rules as configurationEvery campaign has different criteria: which drug and which years, which device, which region. None of that is hard-coded. A campaign is a configuration covering the required questions, disqualifying answers, which registries to check and what the gates are, so a new campaign doesn't need new code.Drift, and why the evidence is mixedIt's adversarial, so it drifts. Once coached callers stop getting through, the coaching changes; some callers started getting small details wrong on purpose to sound more natural. Any fixed set of signals goes stale, which makes recalibration part of routine work.Mixing kinds of evidence helps. The transcript alone catches a lot. Registry checks catch people who've done some homework, and photos catch most of what's left. None of them is decisive alone, but faking all of them at once is hard.And the part that matters most, the session gate, is the least technical part of the system. Check how the interview went before you judge the person on the other end of it.

title: What It Costs to Run mhassan.dev: $8/year
description: The full cost of running this site, what's free, and the tradeoffs behind each choice.
text: My portfolio costs me about $8/year, all of it for the domain. Everything else is free, and the reasons for each pick are below.I wrote this in February 2025, when the site ran on Hugo. In October 2026 I moved it to TanStack Start; the last section covers what changed. The hosting, domain, analytics and comments are the same, and so is the bill.The StackWhatToolCostStatic site generatorHugo + PaperMod (TanStack Start since October 2026)FreeHostingGitHub PagesFreeDomainPorkbun (mhassan.dev)~$8/yearAnalyticsUmami Cloud (hobby plan)FreeCommentsGiscusFreeSSLGitHub Pages auto-provisionFreeWhy Hugo Over Next.js or AstroI tried Astro first and it was fine, but builds took 4 seconds; Hugo builds my entire site in under 200ms. For a markdown blog with no client-side interactivity, that's 4 seconds of complexity I don't need.Hugo also ships no JavaScript by default, so there's nothing to hydrate or bundle. My portfolio loads fast on bad connections because there's almost nothing to load except HTML, CSS, and images.The downside is that Hugo's templating language is ugly. If you've ever written {{ with .Params.cover }}{{ if .image }} you know what I mean. I only touch templates when I'm customizing PaperMod, which is maybe twice a year.Porkbun Over CloudflareCloudflare Registrar is cheaper for some TLDs, but Porkbun gives you free WHOIS privacy and a dashboard that wasn't designed for infrastructure engineers, and the DNS setup for GitHub Pages took about 3 minutes. I set a CNAME record, GitHub provisioned the SSL cert, done.Umami Over Google AnalyticsGoogle Analytics is free too, but it's also a privacy liability, and I don't want a cookie banner on my portfolio. Umami gives me page views, referrers, and device breakdowns, which is everything I look at, without tracking individual users or requiring consent.I use Umami's hosted hobby plan. The dashboard is clean, and it sets no cookies and doesn't fingerprint visitors.Giscus for CommentsGiscus uses GitHub Discussions as a backend. Commenters need a GitHub account, which keeps spam bots out and means comments come from developers. Moderation goes through GitHub's existing tools, with no database, backend, or Disqus ads.Replacing the HomepageThe first thing I changed, eventually, was swapping PaperMod's profile-mode homepage for a custom one. PaperMod is excellent for posts, but a centered avatar and subtitle can only say so much.Leaving HugoIn October 2026 I moved the site to TanStack Start, with the posts as MDX, as part of a full redesign. A command palette, keyboard shortcuts and reading settings followed a few days later. It still prerenders every page to static HTML, so GitHub Pages serves it the same way as before.The cost of leaving Hugo was the thing I'd praised it for. The first build shipped every post to every page, and on a slow phone over 3G a page took about nine seconds to become usable. Splitting each post into its own chunk and loading the palette and other extras on first use took the main bundle from 460 KB to 158 KB gzipped. That's still more JavaScript than Hugo ever sent, and it's the trade I made for the features.

title: Final Year Project (FYP) Guide for Students
description: A practical final year project guide for choosing scope, building steadily, avoiding weak ideas, and presenting work clearly.
text: IntroductionThe fact that you have decided to read this behemoth of an article deserves admiration and tells me that you're serious about your academics and career (or are procrastinating on something else). Give me the next 20 mins of your life and I'll make you into a much more informed individual. Your Final Year Project (FYP) is one of the most important academic tasks in your degree. It can shape your career, fill out your portfolio, and make you better at solving problems.This guide covers how to choose the right topic, advisor, tech stack, and strategy so your FYP stands out. It mainly targets FASTians because that's where my experience is, but the advice applies to any university. I've been through the process as a student, and now I see it from the other side as a lab instructor. So take my very opinionated advice with a grain of salt.Research & Development vs. DevelopmentEarly on, decide which type of project fits your interests, skills, and career goals. There are two broad categories:Research and development (R&D) projects have a theoretical research component plus a practical implementation. Expect to explore new concepts, do literature reviews, and test hypotheses while also building a functional prototype.In pure development projects you build a fully functional product or system using existing technologies and methods, usually with less emphasis on novel research.A quick comparison:AspectR&D ProjectsPure DevelopmentFocusResearch + prototypeBuild a complete productInnovationNovel contributions, possible publicationsApplies proven methodsTime & RiskLonger, uncertain outcomesPredictable, lower riskCareer FitAcademia, research rolesIndustry, hands-on codingDocumentationResearch-heavy reportsTechnical & project docsTip: Pick a Research & Development project if you want to explore new ideas and contribute to academic knowledge and can live with more uncertainty. Pick a Pure Development project if you'd rather build a market-ready product that shows future employers what you can do.How to Choose a TopicPicking the right topic makes or breaks your FYP. A good topic should be:Interesting: Choose something you're passionate about. No one wants to work on a boring project, let alone for a whole year.Feasible: Consider your time, skills, and available resources. Scope is one of the most important factors in your FYP. It will dictate your life for the next year, and it's the first thing your advisor(s) and the evaluation committee will ask you about.Relevant: Align with industry trends or research needs. As an example, I am an avid "AI" pessimist but I can't deny the fact that it's the hottest trend in the industry right now. So, if you're into AI, you might want to consider a project in that domain. Look at the recent explosion of AI Agents and Generative AI. I have many concerns about the ethical implications of these technologies but that's a topic for another day. You want a skillset that's in demand, or at the very least will allow you to have a good conversation with a potential employer. That said, don't pick the next hottest thing and chase after it, because by the time you're done with your project it might not be the hottest thing anymore. Pick something you're passionate about that aligns with your academic and career goals.Problem-Solving: Your project should address a real problem or offer innovation. Please don't build another e-commerce website or a basic recommendation system. A novel project will make you stand out and give you a sense of accomplishment (and probably a few sleepless nights but you're a FASTian, it's your life anyway).Tip: Browse research papers, GitHub projects, and tech blogs for inspiration. Look at what the students from foreign universities are doing. They're not necessarily smarter than you but they have access to better resources and they're more likely to be working on current research problems. You don't have to copy them, but take every chance to learn from them. A good way to shortlist a project is to do a preliminary literature review, which tells you what's already been done and what hasn't. Don't wanna jump into an overcrowded room now, do you?How to Choose an AdvisorYour advisor plays a huge role in your project's success. A good advisor should be:Experienced in your chosen field: If your idea is novel and complex enough, you might want an advisor who has experience in that domain. They can guide you better and help you avoid common pitfalls. A good example is the HODs who excel in their respective fields. They’re usually very busy but if you can get them to agree to be your advisor, you’re in for a treat. There are also many, many other faculty members who are just as good (if not better, considering they have more time to dedicate to you), and you should consider them as well.Responsive and willing to guide you properly: This is a big one. You don’t want an advisor who’s too busy to meet with you or doesn’t respond to your emails. And let me be clear, this isn’t a slight against any of the faculty members; they’re all extremely helpful and knowledgeable. Some of them are just too busy to give you the attention you need. This is where clear communication with your potential advisor comes in. Be upfront about your expectations and ask them about theirs, including their current project load and typical response times.Supportive of your ideas but also critical when needed: Everyone loves a chill time but you shouldn’t try to chill with your FYP. You need someone who can guide you properly and point out the flaws in your project. You need someone who can push you to do better. You need someone who can be your mentor. And you need someone who can be your friend. And you need someone who can be your critic. And you need someone who can be your cheerleader. That was a lot of "ands" but you get the point. FAST is filled with faculty members who can be all of these things and more. You just need to find the right one for you.Co-Advisor: If possible, consider having a co-advisor for a second perspective and more support. This is especially useful if your project needs expertise in multiple domains. For example, if it involves both AI and Web Development, you might want an AI expert as your primary advisor and a Web Development expert as your co-advisor.External Advisor: If you can get an external advisor, that’s even better. Don’t know where to find them? Start with your team leads or managers at the companies you interned at. If you build a trustworthy and professional relationship with them, they might be willing to help you out. They can give you real-world insights, help you align your project with industry needs, and help with your job search after graduation. It always comes down to networking and building relationships. If you provide value to others, they’ll reciprocate (mostly).How to find one?Check faculty profiles and see their published work.Ask seniors about their experiences with different advisors. This is the most important one. They've been through the process and they know who's good and who's not. They can also be biased towards or against certain faculty members, so take their advice with a grain of salt. Maybe the advisor who was too strict for them is the perfect fit for you.Approach multiple advisors with a short, well-prepared proposal. Get a printed copy, please. It's a small thing but it shows that you're serious about your project, and it's a good habit to get into. You should always have a printed copy of your proposal, your project plan, your project report, your project presentation, your project defence, your project... you get the point.Choosing the Right Tech StackYour tech stack should be practical and aligned with your project's scope. Consider:Industry Demand: Is the tech widely used (e.g., Python, React, Django)?Community Support and Libraries: Are there resources available for learning and troubleshooting? Don't pick an obscure tool where you're stuck bashing your head against a wall because there's no documentation. Pick one with a large community behind it, so when you run into an issue a Google search turns up the solution.Scalability: Can your tech handle future growth? Not all projects need to scale. If your project is meant for a small group of people, scalability might not be a concern; if it's meant for a large group, it should be one of your top concerns. So please don't over-engineer or under-engineer your project. I have a habit of designing projects (even hobby ones) that can scale to thousands of users, and that's not always necessary.Learning Curve: Will you have time to master it? FASTians are built different. They can learn anything in a short amount of time. That doesn't mean you should try to learn everything. Stick to what you know and what you can learn in a reasonable amount of time. You don't want to be learning a new language or framework in the middle of your project. Imagine flying a plane with your right while holding the manual on your left. If you have some time before your FYP starts, though, you can use it to learn a new language or framework.Example Tech Stacks:Web Apps: Vue.js / Django / PostgreSQL. I love this stack. It's simple, powerful, and easy to learn.AI/ML: Python (TensorFlow, PyTorch) + Flask / FastAPIMobile Apps: Kotlin / Swift. I prefer native apps to hybrid apps because I want to squeeze every bit of performance out of my apps. You might not care about that, and hybrid is perfectly fine.Tip: Stick to technologies you are comfortable with or have enough time to learn.Can an FYP Help with Employment and Master's Admissions?Yes. A well-executed FYP can:Impress recruiters: Companies prefer candidates who have built real-world projects that they can check out.Boost your resume & portfolio: Especially if it’s on GitHub with good documentation, code quality, a working demo, and a good commit history.Support your Master’s application: A strong project with a research component can help in admissions and scholarships.Tip: Try to publish a paper or present your project in a competition for extra credibility.How to Write a Strong ProposalA solid proposal improves your chances of approval and gives you a roadmap for the project. It should include:Project Title: Clear and concise.Problem Statement: What issue are you solving? Be specific about the challenges or gaps your project addresses.Objectives: Define clear, measurable goals. Instead of a vague aim like "I want to build a website," write "I want to build a website that allows users to register, search, and interact with community content."Tech Stack: Justify your choice of tools. Explain why you picked one database over another, a specific language, or a particular framework. This shows you've researched the technical needs of your project.Expected Outcomes: Describe the expected impact of your project. What problems will it solve, and how will it benefit users or contribute to your field?Methodology: Outline your approach, whether it’s a research-driven study, iterative software development, or an experimental design, so it's clear how you’ll reach your objectives.Literature Review: Give a brief overview of existing work related to your topic. This shows what's new about your project and what it builds on.Timeline & Milestones: Include a realistic timeline with specific milestones. Splitting the project into phases shows you have a plan for finishing on schedule.Risk Management & Contingency Plans: Identify potential challenges, such as technical hurdles or resource constraints, and how you'd handle them. Evaluators like seeing that you've thought ahead.Resource & Budget Considerations (if applicable): Detail any additional resources or funding you may need, such as software licenses, hardware, or access to special datasets.Tip: Avoid overly ambitious goals. "Underpromise and overdeliver" is a solid strategy; overpromising what you can achieve leads to unnecessary stress and setbacks.Project Management Best PracticesA few habits keep the project moving:Use Agile/Scrum: Break work into small, manageable tasks.Version Control: Use Git/GitHub for tracking changes. For the love of all that's holy, don't send each other code files over WhatsApp. Use Git. It's not that hard to learn and it will save you a lot of time and effort.Task Management: Use Trello, Notion, or Jira for planning. You can mostly get away with Trello; it's simple and free. If you want more features, use Notion or Jira.Code Documentation: Write readable, well-commented code. Look into tools that help with this, for example JSDoc for JavaScript, Sphinx for Python, and Doxygen for C++.Usecase-based development: Divide the use cases amongst the members and have each person build theirs end to end. Don't commit the cardinal sin of assigning a whole layer to one member (my X member did the frontend). This is a recipe for disaster.Tip: Meet with your team/advisor weekly to track progress.Testing & Deployment StrategiesTesting is often overlooked, and your project's success depends on it. Plan for:Unit Testing: Test individual components to make sure they work as expected.Integration Testing: Verify that different modules interact correctly.Performance Testing: Measure scalability and speed; look at techniques like skeleton and lazy loading for optimization.Security Testing: Check your application for vulnerabilities, especially if it handles sensitive data.Usability Testing: Get feedback from real users to find out whether the project is easy to use.For deployment:Reliable Platforms: Choose trusted platforms like AWS, Firebase, Heroku, or DigitalOcean. For a more hands-on approach, consider setting up your own VPS.Automated Testing & Deployment: Use CI/CD pipelines to run tests and deploy automatically. This cuts manual errors and keeps releases consistent.Backup & Rollback Plans: Have a documented rollback plan. When a deployment goes wrong, it saves time and can prevent data loss.Tip: Document any issues you hit during testing and deployment, and how you resolved them. Those notes help a lot during your project defence and on future projects.Preparing for Your FYP DefenseYour FYP defence is where you show off your work. A great presentation includes:Clear Project Demo: Focus on the key features and functionality of your project. Prepare backup materials like screenshots or a recorded demo in case of technical glitches.Performance Insights: Present efficiency improvements, benchmarking data, or any performance metrics that back up your claims.Comprehensive Understanding: Every team member should know every part of the project, so you're ready for both technical and theoretical questions from the panel.Presentation Design & Narrative: Keep the slides clear, concise, and easy to look at. Walk through the problem, your approach, and the impact of your project as one story.Handling Q&A: Anticipate common questions and practice your responses. Be ready to discuss challenges, lessons learned, and possible future enhancements.Tip: Practice your defense multiple times before presenting so you stay calm when the unexpected questions come. Make sure all the members know all the details of the project. You don't want to be caught off guard by a question you should know the answer to.Company Sponsorships and Mentorship ProgramsYou can also find support outside your department:If you've interned at a company, approach them with your project proposal. They might be interested in sponsoring your project, providing financial support and making sure your work matches industry needs. This is how it worked for me and how I got my external advisor.Many professors have strong links with software houses. Occasionally, they secure projects from these companies that can be developed as part of a student's FYP. Ask your advisor if such opportunities exist.In Pakistan, several software houses now run FYP mentorship programs. They pair students with experienced industry professionals who advise them throughout the project.Reach out to professionals in your field on LinkedIn. Many are willing to mentor students and advise on project development, tech stack selection, and career opportunities, so even if you can't get into a mentorship program, you can still have a mentor. You just need to ask.Tip: Ask both your past internship supervisors and your professors about these opportunities. They can lead to industry partnerships.One last thingTreat your FYP as a launchpad for your career.Choose the right topic and tech stack.Work with a supportive advisor.Follow best coding & project management practices.Use it to boost your resume and career prospects.Final Tip: Start early, be consistent, and seek feedback from peers and advisors.I hope this guide helps with your Final Year Project. If you have questions, reach out or leave a comment.

title: kitty's Parallel Test Runner Said OK While Its Workers Crashed
description: A missing addSubTest and an ignored exit status let kitty's new parallel test runner report success after failures. Fixing that exposed seven segfaulting workers on my Mac, and Kovid Goyal fixed those his own way.
text:
In August 2026 I was going through kitty, the GPU terminal emulator, looking for things worth a pull request. I had Codex on GPT-5.6 doing a first audit pass over the repo. I picked which findings were worth a maintainer's time and reviewed every line before anything went upstream. Its list had a shell-quoting bug in choose-files at the top, which Kovid Goyal merged on the morning of 12 August. Second on the list was the test runner.kitty had switched to running its Python tests in parallel two weeks earlier (39ae060d2, "Run python test in parallel", 29 July). This post is about a hole in that runner, what showed up once the hole was closed, and the part Kovid fixed himself. (An earlier exchange with Kovid, about hard links, is in the best way to learn a codebase.)How the runner collects resultskitty_tests/main.py splits the test list round-robin into up to eight chunks and calls os.fork() once per chunk. Each child runs its tests with a unittest.TestResult subclass called PipeTestResult, which writes one JSON line per event into a pipe: start, ok, fail, error, skip and so on. The parent reads all the pipes, counts records, prints a progress line like Py 211/406, and at the end decides pass or fail from the records it received.That last decision looked like this:python_ok = not (py_failures or py_errors or py_unexpected_successes or py_worker_errors)So the parent only knew about failures that arrived as records. Anything that failed without writing a record counted as nothing.A failing subTest left no recordPipeTestResult implemented addSuccess, addFailure, addError, addSkip and the expected-failure pair, and it had no addSubTest. When a test uses with self.subTest(...) and one of the subtests fails, unittest calls result.addSubTest() for that subtest. Because the test as a whole didn't succeed, it never calls addSuccess for it either. The base class's addSubTest appends to result.failures inside the child, but nothing goes down the pipe.The parent ended up with a start record for the test and nothing else. A synthetic test with one failing subtest, run through the real collector, printed Ran 0 tests followed by OK, and collect_worker_results() returned success.The child did know it had failed. run_test_worker exited with status 1 when result.failures was non-empty. The parent then threw that away:for pid in pids:
    os.waitpid(pid, 0)kitty's GLFW, drag-and-drop, font and shell-integration tests all use subTest, so a real assertion failure in any of them would have shown up as one fewer test in the count and a green result.The first fixI wanted each channel to mean one thing. The pipe carries test outcomes, including subtests. The exit status says whether the worker process itself survived.def addSubTest(self, test, subtest, err) -> None:
    super().addSubTest(test, subtest, err)
    if err is not None:
        record_type = 'fail' if issubclass(err[0], test.failureException) else 'error'
        self._send({'t': record_type, 'id': str(subtest), 'e': self._elapsed(),
                    'msg': self._exc_info_to_string(err, test)})The worker now exits 0 after running its tests whether they passed or not, since the failures already went through the pipe, and the parent checks every status:for pid in pids:
    _, status = os.waitpid(pid, 0)
    if status != 0:
        py_worker_errors.append(
            f'Python test worker {pid} exited with status {os.waitstatus_to_exitcode(status)}')Without that split, a failing test would be reported twice (once as a test failure, once as a worker failure). The commit was 63 added lines, most of them two regression tests: one for the subtest record, one where a forked child exits 3 and the collector has to say so.Then the full suite went redThe focused tests passed. Then I ran the whole suite on my Mac and got this:  Py 211/406 ✓  Go 248 ✓  [37.6s]
======================================================================
WORKER ERROR
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Python test worker 54290 exited with status -11
...
Ran 459 tests in 37.564s

FAILED (worker errors=7)Seven workers had died with signal 11, and 195 Python tests never ran. The code I had changed only reports crashes, so these had been happening before my change too. Going by the python_ok line above, the unpatched runner would have printed Ran 459 tests and OK for this exact run, with the progress line stuck at 211 of 406.Running the same suite sequentially, with no forking, passed: 406 Python tests and 248 Go tests.macOS writes a crash report for every one of those children, and each had the same two annotations:CoreFoundation:    *** multi-threaded process forked ***
libsystem_c.dylib: crashed on child side of fork pre-execThe faulting stack was a SIGSEGV (KERN_INVALID_ADDRESS) inside a CoreFoundation preferences lookup, _CFPreferencesCopyValueWithContainer, called from os_log_type_enabled. In other words, a child process was asking the logging system whether a log level was enabled, and that lookup touched framework state that hadn't survived the fork.Why fork is risky on macOSPOSIX says that when a multi-threaded process calls fork(), the child gets a copy of the whole address space but only the thread that called fork(). Any lock another thread held at that moment stays locked forever in the child, and any half-updated data structure stays half-updated. So until the child calls one of the exec functions, it is only supposed to call async-signal-safe functions. Running a Python interpreter is far outside that list.Plenty of programs get away with it on Linux. macOS is less forgiving because its system frameworks start their own threads and keep a lot of process-wide state, and CoreFoundation records that a fork happened (that's where the first annotation in the crash reports came from). Python has documented this for years. Since 3.8, multiprocessing defaults to spawn on macOS, and the docs say fork "should be considered unsafe as it can lead to crashes of the subprocess as macOS system libraries may start threads". Since 3.12, os.fork() raises a DeprecationWarning when it can tell the process has multiple threads.The runner did this right before forking:# Pre-initialize fonts once before forking so all worker processes inherit
# the warm C-level fontconfig state and their own all_fonts_map() calls are fast.
from kitty.fonts.common import all_fonts_map

all_fonts_map(True)On Linux that warms fontconfig, which is what the comment is about. On macOS all_fonts_map goes through kitty's CoreText backend, which enumerates fonts through CoreText and CoreFoundation APIs. That was my suspect for how the parent picked up framework state and extra threads before the fork. I didn't prove it, and I should have said so more carefully than I did.My second commit took the blunt route: on macOS, run the Python tests in-process, no forking. I opened kitty#10349, "Report parallel test failures", with both commits (two files, +76/−4).What Kovid did with itHis first reply:Why do you think the test launcher is initializing corefoundation? As far as I know it shouldnt be. And the tests are running fine in macOS in CI and on my mac. I have merged parts of your first commit as they made sense.He had already committed the two halves of the reporting fix to master himself, as 485a12aa12 ("Report python subtest failures when running test suite") and f047fc82d5 ("Report python test worker failures separately from test failures"). Apart from my comment, those diffs are the same as the hunks in my commit. He didn't take the macOS change or my regression-test file.The first draft of my reply conceded the whole diagnosis, which would have made it look like I'd invented a crash. I threw that out. The next version read like a cross-examination, and I threw that out too. What I posted said I'd based the suspicion on the pre-fork all_fonts_map(True) call going through CoreText, gave the machine (an arm64 M5 Pro MacBook Pro, macOS 26.5.1, kitty's bundled Python 3.14.6) and the crash annotations, and agreed that disabling parallel tests on every Mac was too broad if CI and his machine were fine.He answered with a commit, 185de897b4, which on macOS replaces fork() with workers started through subprocess.Popen running kitty +runpy, each getting its test IDs as JSON on stdin and its pipe's file descriptor through pass_fds. The commit message gives the reason as avoiding "CoreFoundation libraries not liking fork + threads", and its Fixes #10349 closed my PR about 40 minutes after I opened it. Linux keeps forked workers.I tested his follow-up cleanup, 00a5ca54ef, twice on the machine that had been crashing. Both runs passed all 395 Python and 247 Go tests, with no worker errors and no new crash reports.Later that day he pushed dcbffe3fe0, which moves the all_fonts_map(True) call into each exec'd worker on macOS and keeps the pre-fork warm-up only on the Linux fork path. On macOS the parent process no longer touches the font code at all during a test run. The commit message calls it a cleanup, and I read it as one, but it does remove the call I'd pointed at from the macOS parent.So the reporting fix came from my PR and he applied it, and the crash fix is his, done a better way than mine. Exec'd workers keep the parallelism and make the fork question irrelevant. My version gave up the parallelism on every Mac to avoid a crash I thought only my Mac had.macOS CI had the same crashI assumed my machine was the odd one out, and while writing this up I went back to kitty's CI logs to check. It wasn't. On the commit I had audited, both macOS jobs reported 173 of 394 Python tests and passed, while the Linux job in the same run got through all 394. Once the change that reports worker exits landed on master, the next macOS runs went red within minutes: three workers died with SIGSEGV in one job and three with SIGABRT in the other, and Linux stayed green. After the switch to exec'd workers, both macOS jobs ran all 395.CI had looked healthy for the same reason my first run did, because the runner ignored how its workers exited. The CI runners were on macOS 26.5.2, which also rules out my point release as the explanation. What I still don't know is what made the parent process multi-threaded before the fork. The crashing stack in my reports went through os_log preference loading, with no font code in the frames I captured, and I never tested the all_fonts_map() theory on its own. Exec'd workers made the question moot.Counting what didn't runThe information was on screen the whole time. The progress line said 211 of 406, and the summary printed Ran 459 tests without comparing it to the 654 the run started with. If I write a runner like this again, the parent will compare the number of results it received against the number of tests it handed out, and treat any gap as a failure, independent of exit codes. An exit status only tells you a worker died. A count also catches a worker that stopped early for some reason nobody has thought of yet.

title: LangChain in Production: What the Tutorials Leave Out
description: Where LangChain is worth using, where it gets in the way, and the defaults that stop our AI features failing silently: timeouts, validation, persistent state, tracing and pinned versions.
text: LangChain tutorials tend to stop at a tidy script that queries a PDF. You think you'll ship it by Friday, and a few weeks later you're working out why a chain returns an empty string with no error.I've shipped LangChain-based features at WebNoodle and at Entropy Labs, and we still use it for Obelisk's agents. This post covers where I've found it worth the dependency and what I now do by default when I use it.When to use itLangChain is worth it when there's real orchestration: several model calls, tools, branching, approvals, state that has to survive a pause. The agent and middleware layer handles a lot of plumbing you'd otherwise write badly yourself, and the tracing integration is good.For "summarize this text", a direct SDK call is shorter, easier to debug and one less dependency to upgrade. At Entropy we use the framework for agent workflows and the provider SDK for simple completions.Timeouts and retriesA model call without a timeout will eventually hang a worker. Set one on every model you construct, and put retries on the calls that can safely be repeated:model = init_chat_model(MODEL_NAME, timeout=30, max_retries=2)Be careful what "retry" means once tools are involved. Retrying a timeout is fine. Retrying a tool call that sent an email means sending it twice. In agents, retries belong in middleware that knows which errors are transient; I wrote about that in agent middleware.Checking prompts and resultsThe worst LangChain bug I shipped didn't raise anything. A prompt template rendered an empty message list, the model returned nothing, and the chain reported success. The war stories have the details. Since then, anything important gets checked on both sides: before the call, that the rendered prompt isn't empty, and after it, that the result is non-empty and parses into what you expected. Structured output with a schema does most of the second part for you.Conversation stateThe old in-memory conversation helpers were convenient and wrong for production. State vanished on restart, grew without limit and wasn't safe across concurrent requests. They've since moved to the legacy package in LangChain 1.0, which says enough.Persist state somewhere that outlives a deploy. For agents that means a checkpointer backed by PostgreSQL, keyed by a thread ID, so a conversation can pause for a human approval and pick up hours later. For plain chat history, Redis with an expiry is fine. Either way, you get to decide how long history lives and when it's trimmed.TracingTurn tracing on before the first user, and record every call with its latency, token counts, inputs and outputs. LangSmith is the easy path. We also send our own structured events with a request ID, so a trace, a log line and a user's complaint can be matched to each other. Alert on spend too, because a tool loop that nobody caps will find your budget before you do.VersionsLangChain moves quickly: import paths change, classes move between packages and defaults shift. Pin exact versions, upgrade on purpose, read the release notes, and keep a small smoke test that runs a real chain end to end, so an upgrade breaks in CI instead of in production.
