title: Obelisk
description: An AI marketing platform where specialist agents write, plan and analyze from a company's own material, without leaking one customer's brand into another's.
text: Obelisk is the platform we build at Entropy Labs for marketing teams. A company uploads what it already has (brand guidelines, past campaigns, product docs, analytics access) and gets a set of specialist agents that work from it: brand voice, SEO, email, paid ads, strategy and more.I lead the product and wrote most of the backend. The agents are what people see; most of my time has gone into the code around them.Splitting the general agentEarly Obelisk had one general agent with an enormous prompt. It wrote ad copy when asked about analytics and started research when someone wanted a one-line answer. Splitting it into specialists, each with a short prompt and a small set of tools, fixed most of that.Running more than fifteen of them is manageable because every model and tool call passes through a shared middleware layer. It chooses the model per request, trims long conversations, caps runaway tool loops, retries only what's safe to retry, and asks a human before anything that sends or spends. I wrote about that layer in more detail in agent middleware.Retrieval fast enough to wait forAn agent can only work from what it knows about the company, so retrieval runs before almost every answer. The first version did it in sequence: search the documents, then the saved URLs, then the company profile, then assemble. People waited a long time for the first word.Now the independent lookups run at the same time, and a fast, cheap model rewrites the question before the search so the search returns better material. The rewrite adds a moment and saves several. Documents go through a structure-aware pipeline on the way in, so each chunk is a coherent section of the document.Keeping one customer's brand out of another'sObelisk is multi-tenant: organizations contain spaces, and a space is the unit of isolation. A leak in an AI product is harder to spot than a wrong row in a table. It shows up as another company's tone, or a fact from their documents, inside your draft.So the space is enforced at every layer. The request layer checks it, every repository scopes its queries by it, and cache keys and log lines carry it. Middleware on its own would miss the one query that forgets the scope, and that query is where leaks come from.Sessions that survive restartsSome agent sessions run long, with research, drafts, approvals and revisions. They have to survive deploys, dropped connections and a person coming back the next morning. Conversation state is checkpointed in PostgreSQL, and every step of an agent run is recorded as an event, so a reconnecting client can replay what it missed and we can reconstruct what an agent saw when it did something odd.If I started it againI'd build the control layer first. We added middleware to working agents over months, and it should have been the foundation.Structured logs from the first commit, with request IDs and one event per step, would have saved a lot of long debugging sessions early on.I'd treat prompt injection as a property of the whole system. Pattern checks on inputs and outputs catch the lazy attempts. The damage is limited by structure: agents that can only reach their own tools, a human in front of anything that sends or spends, and retrieved documents treated as data, never as instructions.

title: October
description: A campaign platform where brands, agencies and creators run influencer campaigns from brief to report, with numbers every side can trust.
text: October is where brands, agencies and creators run influencer campaigns together. A brand or its agency sets up a campaign, brings in creators, agrees on deliverables, tracks the posts as they go live and ends up with a report. I lead the product and wrote most of the backend and frontend.It looks like a dashboard product. Most of the engineering went into who can see what, whether the numbers hold up, and keeping the realtime parts safe.Three parties, one set of recordsThe same campaign looks different to each side. A brand sees its campaigns and the creators on them. An agency sees the brands it manages and the creators in its roster. A creator sees their own work, across every brand and agency they deal with.The difficult cases sit in between. A creator profile can be imported by an agency before the creator ever signs up, then claimed by the real person later. The claim has to attach to the right profile, keep the history, and not expose the agency's private data to the creator or the other way round. Rosters have owners, imports go through a review step before they count, and every query is scoped to the role asking, not just to the account.Numbers you can put in front of a clientCampaign reports go to people who pay for campaigns, so a number that's "roughly right" is a problem. A lot of the work before launch went into making every count on every dashboard and export come from verified records: posts that were approved and linked, never estimates, placeholders or whatever the last sync happened to return.That sounds obvious and took a lot of work. Previews are bounded so a big roster doesn't make a dashboard crawl, and the summary numbers are cached, but they come from the same verified records.Realtime that fails safelyMessaging and live dashboards run over WebSockets. Browsers can't send normal auth headers on a socket, so connections authenticate with short-lived opaque tickets issued over the regular API. Reconnects always fetch a fresh ticket, and idle connections are cleaned up so they don't sit holding server resources.AI where it's cheap to be wrongOctober uses AI for recommendations, like which creators might suit a brief. The work is bounded in time and size, runs off the request path where it can, and only ever suggests. Nobody gets added to a campaign because a model said so.If I started it againI'd model the roles before the screens. The permission model kept changing as we learned how agencies work, and writing it down first, as rules with tests, would have made those changes cheaper.I'd decide what counts as a fact early. "What exactly are we counting?" was a product question we answered in code too late.

title: PixelCryptor: Hiding Executables Inside Images
description: A Django project that embeds executable files within images using delimiter-based concatenation, and why real steganography is harder than this.
text:
PixelCryptor is a Django app that lets you embed an executable file inside an image. Upload both files, it concatenates them with a delimiter, and stores the result on Azure Blob Storage. You can later extract the original files back out.How It WorksThe approach is deliberately simple: append the executable bytes to the image bytes with a known delimiter between them.def obfuscate_images(image_blob_name, executable_blob_name):
    image_data = image_blob_client.download_blob().readall()
    executable_data = executable_blob_client.download_blob().readall()

    delimiter = b"---EXECUTABLE_BOUNDARY---"
    obfuscated_data = image_data + delimiter + executable_data

    obfuscated_blob_client.upload_blob(obfuscated_data, overwrite=True)Image formats like JPEG and PNG store their data length in headers. Most viewers stop reading at the image data boundary, so the appended executable bytes are invisible when you open the file as an image. Deobfuscation finds the delimiter and splits the bytes back apart.Why This Is Naive (And That's the Point)Real steganography hides information in the pixel data itself, usually by modifying the least significant bits, so it stays undetectable even under statistical analysis. This project concatenates bytes. Anyone who looks at the file size or runs hexdump will see the appended data straight away.I built it as a university project to understand binary file manipulation, Azure Blob Storage integration, and Django file handling. The "obfuscation" was the least interesting part. I got more out of learning how image formats define their data boundaries and why appending arbitrary bytes doesn't corrupt the image.The Azure IntegrationFiles are stored in and retrieved from Azure Blob Storage. The upload/download logic is straightforward. What took care was getting binary data through Django's file upload pipeline without corrupting bytes: request.FILES gives you UploadedFile objects that need to be read as binary, not decoded as text.The source is on GitHub.

title: Polaris
description: Retail operations software for shops that bill all day: invoices, refunds, batch stock, supplier orders and customer ledgers that have to agree with each other.
text: Polaris started as client work through Commit Software and turned into the system several retail shops run their day on. It covers the parts a shop touches constantly: invoices and quotations, refunds, stock, customer credit, supplier purchasing, expenses, reports, and the admin around all of it.Most of the work is in the edge cases. A billing screen has to stay right when two cashiers sell the last item, a customer returns half an order on credit, and a supplier's price list arrives as a scanned PDF.Stock derived from batchesA product's quantity is always derived from batch records, never typed in: what came in, from whom, at what cost, and what's left. That rule made every other module stricter. Billing, restocking, cycle counts and supplier returns all have to go through the same contract, and none of them can "just fix the number".It costs more work up front, and it's why stock counts in Polaris can be trusted at the end of the day.Several cashiers at onceThe race conditions came first, as they do. Two cashiers selling the last unit took stock negative, and two operations on one customer could leave a balance that matched neither. The war stories post has the details. These are the fixes that stuck:row locks that fail fast and retry briefly instead of queueing, so a cashier sees a blip at worstversion checks, so a stale form can't overwrite newer editsper-customer and per-supplier advisory locks for ledger work, with keys that mean the same thing on every worker processtests that pin those contracts down, including one that checks lock keys come out the same under different hash seedsTenants separated in the databasePolaris is multi-tenant. The organization is set once per request and carried down into the database session, so the separation doesn't depend on every query remembering a filter.Supplier files arrive however suppliers likePrice lists come as CSV, Excel and PDF, with inconsistent names, missing units and layouts that change without warning. The import path extracts, normalizes and matches them against the catalogue, with aliases for the names suppliers insist on using. It locks around anything that can change purchasing, because a half-applied price list is worse than none.If I started it againI'd write explicit services from the start. Early versions spread business rules across Django signals; they're now plain service functions you can read top to bottom. The performance log covers that and the other early mistakes.Concurrency tests on day one. Every serious bug in Polaris was a concurrency bug that a two-thread test would have caught.A written contract for every module boundary, since the worst bugs lived in the gaps between modules.

title: mhassan.dev — This Portfolio
description: TanStack Start, React, typed MDX content, accessible controls, and static GitHub Pages output. How the site is built.
text: This portfolio runs on TanStack Start, React and TypeScript. The build produces static HTML for GitHub Pages, so there's no application server to host.Application and contentTanStack Router owns navigation, route loaders, page metadata and search parameters. Content Collections validates the MDX and shared profile data against strict Zod schemas, then generates TypeScript types. Profile facts live in one place, data/profile.yaml.Page components use those types directly. Buttons and inputs are shadcn controls built on Base UI. Search runs Fuse over the published content catalog and keeps the query in the URL.Loading only what a page needsThe app bundle carries metadata for every page, and each page body is its own chunk. Route loaders fetch the body, and the build preloads it in that page's prerendered HTML, so content never waits on hydration. Search text loads on demand. The command palette, dialogs, mobile menu, toasts and easter eggs load the first time someone opens them. That took the main bundle from 460 KB to 158 KB gzipped, and an article page now loads 165 KB of JavaScript, down from over 450 KB.On weak machines, or with Save-Data on, the site sets data-perf="low" and drops repaint-heavy hover transitions, backdrop blur and page cross-fades.Static outputTanStack Start discovers routes and follows internal links during prerendering. The output includes authored pages and topic collections. Build scripts generate feeds, the sitemap, redirects, the search index, per-page chunk preloads and a standalone 404 from the same catalog.Before deployment, verification checks the published URL contract, page content, metadata, structured data, internal links, feeds and the sitemap.Comments and analyticsGiscus maps page paths to GitHub Discussions. Umami counts page views. Both kept their configuration through the move off Hugo.Development and publishingpnpm dev builds the content types and starts Vite. pnpm verify checks types, lint, design tokens, formatting and copy, then builds the site and checks the output and public URLs. The GitHub Actions workflow installs the locked dependencies, runs verification, and publishes dist/client on pushes to main.The earlier version used Hugo and PaperMod. Their templates, configuration, theme submodule and runtime are gone, and every existing public path still resolves; the build checks them against a fixed list.

title: RISQ
description: Scoring intake calls for mass tort firms: separating real claimants from coached callers, with evidence a reviewer can follow.
text: Mass tort firms take a lot of calls from people who might qualify for a case. Some callers are coached, some never used the product, some call back under another name. RISQ listens to each intake call and recommends whether to send the caller on to a closer, flag them for review, or quarantine the call.The interesting parts are how it scores, and why the score that matters most measures the interviewer rather than the caller. I've written that up in detail in Scoring fraud in legal intake calls. This page is the short version.Separate questions before a verdictRISQ asks four questions separately: does the caller remember real detail, does the story sound like their own, do they meet the campaign's criteria, and did the intake agent ask good questions. Only the first three feed the recommendation. The fourth is a gate: a poor interview makes honest people sound rehearsed, so RISQ refuses to judge the caller when the interview itself was bad.Evidence from more than one directionA call is transcribed with the speakers separated, then an LLM extracts structured claims: which product, when, which doctors and facilities. Doctors and facilities are checked against public registries. For some campaigns the caller is asked to text a photo, and a vision model checks it's what it claims to be. No signal decides on its own, and faking all of them at once is hard.Decisions a reviewer can followThe recommendation comes out of a sequence of gates, and each call stops at the first one it fails. When a call is quarantined, the reviewer sees the gate that stopped it and why.

title: Teaching
description: What I taught at FAST-NUCES, how I like to teach, and where students can start.
text: I taught labs at FAST-NUCES from 2024 to 2025, in Operating Systems, Software Construction and Development, and Web Engineering. Before that I was a teaching assistant for two years, for Software Engineering, Mobile Development, Information Security and Software Project Management.The best moments came when someone's clean solution stopped working and they had to trace what happened instead of guessing. A lot of what I tried to teach was that habit.How I like to teachStart from a real system, one that can break.Make people debug before they get the answer.Talk about tradeoffs, because the textbook answer is usually one of several.Keep explanations plain, and assume edge cases count.For studentsThe FYP guide is the long, opinionated version of what I told final-year students every semester.Free web dev platforms worth your time, if you're starting out.The best way to learn a codebase is about what open source teaches that coursework doesn't.If you want help with a project, a workshop or a talk, email hi@mhassan.dev.
